The salt spray tasted of regret. Elias traced patterns in the condensation on his window, the persistent drumming a mournful rhythm against the glass. He hadn’t seen rain like this in years, not since he’d… well, since he’d left. The town was swallowed in grey, the harbor a churning slate mirroring the turmoil in his gut. But the old charm, the persistent pull of the coast, had proven too strong. 

He’d come back for the archives, purportedly to catalog the collection of maritime charts and logs for the historical society. A perfectly reasonable explanation, one that even he almost believed. The truth was simpler: he needed to see it again, to feel the wind biting at his face, to hear the cries of the gulls echoing off the cliffs. To stand on the edge, as he used to. 

The house felt smaller than he remembered, the rooms crowded with the ghosts of his childhood. His mother’s crochened doilies lay undisturbed on dusty tables, a silent testament to a life lived meticulously, predictably. He’d always resented that order, that predictability. He'd yearned for the wildness of the waves, the unpredictable dance of the tides. He’d chased it relentlessly, taking a job on a research vessel, sailing the world, avoiding the anchor of familiarity.

He pulled open the drawers, each revealing a forgotten corner of a past he’d tried to bury. A tarnished silver compass, tucked away with a faded photograph of his father, a gruff, silent man who’d spent his days piloting boats out of harbor.  A box of sea shells, meticulously collected and labeled, collected by a girl who’d loved the ocean. He stopped at a small, wooden chest, its wood darkened with age. Inside, nestled amongst several dried flowers, was a small, hand-drawn map.

The map was of the coastline, but not the official charts he’D been hired to catalog. This one was much more personal, sketched with a child’s unsteady hand. It charted not locations, but feelings. A heart drawn over a cove where he’d built sandcastle fortresses. A tear next to a stretch of beach where his dog had gotten lost. A vibrant sun over the highest point, a vantage point he knew well. A spot marked with an "X" near the head of the cliffs, simply labeled “Safe”. 

He traced the line from the “X” down to the curve of the coast, his finger lingering on the spot where the harbor met the open sea. A wave of sadness, sharp and unexpected, crashed over him. He hadn’t truly escaped the sea, not really. He’d just been trying to run from a memory, a memory that always mirrored his coastline.

He folded the map carefully, returning it to its chest, his breath suspended. He knew then that he couldn’t stay, not truly. The past held a tidal power, a constant pull towards the shore. He would document the charts and charts, then return to the ocean. But this time, he wouldn't run.




He took one last look at the photographs, a quiet goodbye to the ghosts of the past. 




He turned, the rain stopped and a single gull wheeled overhead.
